 “Qing Court in Four Seasons: Life and Culture of the Imperial Household” Thematic Exhibition Talk | Cultural Exchanges through Tibetan Buddhism Ritual Implements 
 Talk 
 05.11.2026 
 11:00 am–12:00 pm 
 Merit Hall, Palace Academy 
 Tibetan Buddhist ritual implements are commonly used in Buddhist practice, religious ceremonies, and the adornment of temples. The Palace Museum houses more than 10,000 Tibetan Buddhist ritual implements, including objects produced by the Imperial Workshops of the Qing Court and offerings from the Mongolian and Tibetan regions. These ritual implements embody the cultural traditions of the Han, Manchu, Mongolian, and Tibetan peoples, while also reflecting influences from foreign cultures.
 This talk focuses on two right-spiralling conches featured in the thematic exhibition “Qing Court in Four Seasons: Life and Culture of the Imperial Household”, which were presented by the Sixth Panchen Lama to the Qianlong Emperor. Taking them as a starting point, the talk will guide audiences to examine the Tibetan Buddhist ritual implements, and gain insight into the interactions, exchanges, and integration among different peoples, as well as the historical contexts of mutual learning among cultures.
 This talk accompanies the thematic exhibition “Qing Court in Four Seasons: Life and Culture of the Imperial Household”, which will be on view in Gallery 2 at the Hong Kong Palace Museum from 4 November 2026 to 3 November 2028. This exhibition is jointly organised by the Hong Kong Palace Museum and The Palace Museum.

 Wen Ming
 Associate Director
Department of Palace Life and Imperial Ritual
The Palace Museum
 Wen Ming holds a master’s degree in history from Peking University and is a Research Fellow at The Palace Museum. His research focuses on ethnic artefacts and historical archives in The Palace Museum’s collection. He specialises in the historical interpretation, narrative construction, and public communication of objects related to Tibet and Xinjiang, with particular attention to their significance to the shared history of the Chinese national community.
 Wen Ming has extensive academic research and practical experience. He served as chief editor of The Garden of Cining Palace and participated in the compilation of original display reports on Qing palaces, including Fanhualou . He has published more than ten articles in leading academic journals, including Palace Museum Journal and China Tibetology . His representative research includes “A Study on the Tangka of Eighteen Arhats of the Fori Building”, “A Study of the Thangkas in the Main Hall of the First Floor of the Baoxianglou”, “A Comparative Study between the Tsa-tsas enshrined in Xianruo Guan, Cining Garden, The Forbidden City, and Eulogies to the Sacred Images of the Buddhas and Boddhisattvas ( Zhufo-pusa shengxiang zan )”. His research has been widely cited within the academic community.
